Unit K11.317 (K. XI 317). ENGLISH:
GALEN, ON LEECHES, REVULSION, THE CUPPING-GLASS, AND INCISION AND SCARIFICATION. Some people, having caught leeches, shut them up and use them on many occasions. For these, having been made gentle, readily attach themselves to the flesh. Those newly caught, however, should be kept for one day, with a little blood put in for their sustenance; for in this way their venomous matter will be squeezed out. At the time of use, let the part that is to be leeched first be cleansed with nitre and smeared, or scratched with the nails; for they will attach more readily.

Unit K11.317-318 (K. XI 317–318). ENGLISH:
One must put them into lukewarm water and a clean, wide vessel; then, taking them up in a sponge and cleaning off the slimy matter, we shall apply them by hand. After they have fastened on, we pour lukewarm oil over the part so that it does not grow cold. In the case of the hands or feet, the part itself should be put into the water in which the leeches are. If they take hold only slightly, one should snip off their tails with scissors; for as the blood flows out they do not stop drawing until we sprinkle salt or ash on their mouths. After they have fallen off, the venomous matter should be drawn out with a cupping-glass; failing that, one should foment with sponges. As for the bodies (σώματα), if they ooze a little, cumin or meal is to be sprinkled on, and then a little oil is to be bound on with wool. If there is a haemorrhage, linen cloths soaked in vinegar are to be laid on, or burnt oak-gall; or one should soak a sponge in liquid pitch, burn it and apply it. One must know that leeches do not draw the blood that is in the depth, but suck in only the blood that lies next to the flesh.

We use them in place of cupping-glasses, and we pull them off whenever we judge that half the portion of the blood has been drawn. And we also hinder it and do not allow it to flow off until a sufficient amount has been discharged, since the part is chilled both by the leeches, which are cold by nature, and by the ambient air. On revulsion. The most violent influxes of the humours we prevent, by revulsive remedies, from settling down all at once. Revulsive remedies, in the case of an inclination towards the thorax and the belly, are [those that draw] to the hands; vomitings, in the case of one towards the lower parts, just as also the [revulsion] by means of the more acrid clysters [is revulsive] of the [inclination] towards vomitings. Both these inclinations, I mean those through the upper and the lower belly, you will draw back towards urine and sweats; and indeed you will also draw back urine towards sweats and evacuations of the bowel. The cupping-glass applied beside the breasts is also a revulsive remedy. With those fixed upon the hypochondrium you will draw back the rush of the blood towards the nostrils, as also the immoderate flow through the uterus.

Unit K11.319-320 (K. XI 319–320). ENGLISH:
Acrid drugs applied to the hollows (κόλποις) also draw away by revulsion the inclinations of the humours toward the head and the viscera. And in general, revulsion is to be made, for humours flowing upward, toward the lower parts, and for those flowing toward the lower parts, the opposite; and for inward inclinations, outward, and again for outward ones, inward; and if the inclination is toward the right, toward the left, and if toward the left, toward the opposite side. So too backward inclinations are to be drawn forward, and forward ones backward. On the cupping-glass. Cupping-glasses are useful when the body has first been evacuated; for when patients are plethoric we shall not use them. By the same reasoning, in inflammations of the brain and the meninges too we shall not use cupping-glasses at the beginning of the affections, just as we shall not with any other inflamed part either, but only when nothing is any longer flowing in and we have first evacuated the whole body, and there arises a need either to set in motion and lever out what is inflamed, or to draw it toward the outside. While the affections are still coming into being, the cupping-glass is to be applied not to the very limbs that are beginning to suffer, but to the parts continuous with them, for the sake of revulsion.

Unit K11.320-321 (K. XI 320–321). ENGLISH:
At the beginning, however, one must use repellent remedies. The cupping-glass is able to evacuate the matter, relieve pain, diminish inflammation, disperse an inflation with pneuma, restore the appetites, make an atonic stomach toned, deliver from faintings, transfer fluxes out of the depths and dry them, check haemorrhages, draw off the destructive powers of the menses, and lighten the menses. On Incision and Scarification. We shall incise parts of the body that are inflamed, or becoming scirrhous, or distended, or painful, or that have received a flux, when the flux has already come to a standstill; or when acrid matter lies alongside; or when a venomous power has fallen upon them from outside; or when we wish to transfer the matter from some parts to another. For instance, we scarify the legs when the head is affected, or when we wish to diminish matter that is in excess in the body, and especially when the excess has arisen through the retention of matter that is habitually accustomed to be excreted.

Unit K11.321-322 (K. XI 321–322). ENGLISH:
For example, when haemorrhoids have been suppressed, we incise the legs, having first bathed [the patient], or fomenting either with hot [water] or with a sponge. For I have not considered it suitable to divide a vein many times in the year, since the vital pneuma is excreted together with a large quantity of blood. And when this is consumed rather frequently, the whole bulk [of the body] is chilled and all the psychic functions become worse. For this reason the withdrawal must be made from the less important [parts], such as the legs. Incision also benefits eyes chronically affected by flux, and affections of the head, and conditions about the chest and the upper back, and synanchai and impactions (sphēnōseis).
